# Genesis 21 – Research notes

**Gaps:** I found nothing from Orthodox (oca.org) or Pentecostal sites (only Guzik's enduringword.com), and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. NET Bible notes appear only for vv. 1 and 14. The Precept Austin page stopped loading after verse 1, so its later notes are only in short search snippets. Ellicott's main page wouldn't load; his notes come from snippets of pages that quote him.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik says the promise took 25 years to come true, and it came true not because Abraham was perfect in his obedience, but because God was faithful to His Word. He separates God's conditional promises from his unconditional ones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- The Hebrew word for "attended to" (*paqad*) means God stepping in with a purpose, not a casual visit. Precept Austin compares God "visiting" Hannah (1 Sam. 2:21). It also quotes a NET note: the word marks God's special attention, and a person's destiny changes when the LORD "visits." https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-21-commentary
- Kidner (quoted there) says the plain style, which keeps repeating what God had "said" and "spoken," shows how quietly and exactly God is in control. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-21-commentary

**v. 2**
- Guzik lists ways Isaac pictures Christ. One is that both births occurred at God's appointed time (Genesis 21:2; Galatians 4:4). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**v. 3**
- The name Isaac first served as a rebuke of the laughter of Abraham and Sarah (Genesis 17:17-19, 18:12-15), but God turned a gentle rebuke into an occasion for joy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Matthew Henry notes that Ishmael later laughed at Isaac, and that "God's favourites" are often mocked by the world. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm

**v. 4**
- Isaac was the first person to be circumcised on the eighth day according to God's instructions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-21-commentary
- Bridgeway: the circumcision showed that Isaac was heir to God's covenant promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-9.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Henry: when God gives a gift we had stopped hoping for, we should remember our earlier doubting with sorrow. He points out that Sarah had first laughed in disbelief. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm
- Bible.org notes that "children" in v. 7 is plural. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-21

**v. 8**
- Guzik: ancient estimates of weaning age run from 3 to 12 years, but the most reliable research indicates an age of three. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Steven Cole puts Isaac at about two or three, which would make Ishmael about 16. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-43-joy-and-pain-life-faith-genesis-211-21

**v. 9 – How bad was the "mocking"? Commentators really differ here**
- *The wordplay:* the word is the same root as Isaac's name ("laughter"), in a stronger form. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/genesis-21.html
- *Calvin (Reformed):* it was a malignant expression of scorn, by which the forward youth manifested his contempt for his infant brother. Both boys are "sons of laughter," but in opposite senses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-9.html
- *Gill (Baptist):* the quarrel was probably about the inheritance. Ishmael may even have come to blows with Isaac, which is why Paul could call it persecution. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-9.html
- *Adam Clarke (Methodist), the milder view:* Paul calls it persecuting, but Clarke thinks it was probably no more than some kind of ridicule, perhaps about Sarah's age. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-9.html
- *Ellicott, in between:* we may set aside readings that charge Ishmael with gross wickedness, because then sending him away would not have grieved Abraham so much. Still, Paul's word shows Sarah had good reason. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/genesis-21.html
- *Keil & Delitzsch:* the causes were unbelief, envy and pride. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-13.html
- *Henry:* he draws a lesson about the lasting hostility between the serpent's offspring and the woman's offspring. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm
- *Ligonier (R.C. Sproul's ministry):* the word "often has sinister overtones," and Ishmael probably lacked faith. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/fleshly-persecution
- *Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):* the article on Isaac renders the word "playing" and asks what Sarah actually saw. It suggests the mere sight of Ishmael may have provoked her. Because the expulsion comes right after the weaning, it also raises the possibility that Hagar was Isaac's wet nurse. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/isaac/
- *A debated popular application:* one sermon quoted on Precept Austin traces the Middle East hostilities today back to this mocking. It treats Isaac as the Jewish people and Ishmael's descendants as Muslims. https://www.preceptaustin.org/genesis-21-commentary

**vv. 10–12 – Paul's allegory (Gal. 4): each tradition reads it differently**
- *Calvin:* God told Abraham to listen to Sarah because God was using her to confirm his own promise. Sending Ishmael away carried out "In Isaac shall thy seed be called." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/galatians/4-30.html
- *Luther (Lutheran):* in the allegory Abraham represents God. Abraham had two sons, born respectively of Hagar and Sarah. The two women represent the two Testaments. https://ccel.org/ccel/luther/galatians/galatians.vii.html
- *Modern Lutheran (1517.org):* the allegory is about "two kinds of righteousness." Ishmael's birth was a human plan to do God's work. https://www.1517.org/articles/understanding-pauls-allegory-of-hagar-and-sarah
- *Spurgeon (Baptist):* Hagar stands for the covenant of works. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons02/sermons02.xv.html
- *Desiring God (John Piper's ministry):* Abraham and Hagar tried to gain the blessing in their own strength, which Piper compares to Sinai. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/hagar-and-slavery-vs-sarah-and-freedom
- *Guzik:* there can be no peaceful coexistence with the flesh. The legalists – represented by Ishmael – have always persecuted true Christianity, represented by Isaac. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/galatians-4/
- *Henry:* the passage points to God rejecting the unbelieving Jews for persecuting the infant church. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm
- *Catholic/Orthodox, Chrysostom (newadvent.org):* Hagar is the type of the earthly Jerusalem, Sarah the Church. The once-barren woman is the Church of the Gentiles, and the other is the synagogue. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/23104.htm
- *A different view of Sarah:* Bible.org (Steven Cole) and the Hagar series there see Sarah's resentment as the source of the trouble. Coffman instead defends Sarah and says she knew what she was doing. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-hagar-pt-2-when-troubles-won-t-go-away-gen-218-21 ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-9.html

**v. 11**
- Henry: Abraham was grieved both by Ishmael's behaviour and by how severe Sarah's demand was. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm
- Guzik: Abraham may have kept Ishmael as a "backup plan," and God wanted him to trust God alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**v. 13**
- God was not against Ishmael. His descendants became the Arab peoples. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**v. 14 – Was Abraham's provision faithful or half-hearted? Opinions differ**
- *Ligonier:* Abraham obeys, but he does so half-heartedly, with hardly enough supplies. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/god-rescues-ishmael
- *Guzik:* Abraham knew no amount of supplies would be enough without God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- *Geneva Bible note:* True faith renounces all natural affections to obey God's commandment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-14.htm
- *Was Ishmael carried?* Keil & Delitzsch say he was 15 or 16, not an infant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-14.htm The NET note says the Hebrew wording about "the boy" is unclear. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Gen+21%3A14%2C21 Bible.org takes "on her shoulder" as an idiom for getting ready for a journey. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-21
- *Modern scholarship (Bible Odyssey):* Abraham leaves them with minimal provision, and Hagar's status as a slave decides her fate. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/hagar/

**vv. 15–16**
- Ligonier: Hagar laying the boy under a bush and moving out of earshot shows how desperate things were. Only God could rescue them. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/god-rescues-ishmael
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: Christians should feel the same compassion for souls perishing without Christ. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**v. 17**
- God answered the boy's voice rather than Hagar's weeping, so Guzik concludes Ishmael himself cried out for help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Henry: we read of no words from the boy, but his groans "cried aloud in the ears of mercy." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_021.cfm

**v. 18**
- Barnes: this renews the promise of Genesis 16:10. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-20.html

**v. 19**
- Guzik: whether God created a spring or showed her one already there, he provided. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Henry: there is a "well" near us in the covenant of grace that we don't see until God opens our eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-14.htm

**vv. 20–21**
- Bible.org: the bowshot that once separated Ishmael from his mother becomes the skill he lives by. https://bible.org/seriespage/2-hagar-pt-2-when-troubles-won-t-go-away-gen-218-21
- Calvin: Ishmael let his mother choose his wife, keeping the order nature itself teaches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/21-20.html
- Henry: Paran was a wild place, suited to a wild man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-14.htm

**vv. 22–24**
- Guzik: this Abimelech was probably not the one in chapter 20, since "Abimelech" may be a royal title. The king noticed God's presence in Abraham's life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**vv. 25–30**
- Wells were vital land in Canaan, so Abraham rightly protested. The animals may have been covenant sacrifices. When Abimelech accepted the seven lambs, he was acknowledging that Abraham dug the well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Henry: Abraham made sure his right to the well was recognised, to prevent future disputes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-33.htm

**v. 31**
- Beersheba can mean "well of seven" or "well of the oath." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/

**v. 32**
- Barnes: Beer-sheba was on the borders of the land of the Philistines. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/genesis-21.html

**v. 33**
- A tamarisk takes a long time to grow, so planting one showed Abraham trusted God's promise of the land. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-21/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the long-lived tree was a type of God's ever-enduring covenant grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-33.htm
- Clarke: this is the first place Scripture uses *olam* ("everlasting") as a quality of God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/ice/ilb/genesis/21-33.html
- The Septuagint and old versions struggled with the word for tamarisk: the Septuagint has "field," and the KJV and Douay have "grove." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-33.htm

**v. 34**
- Henry: Abraham stayed because he had good neighbours. He openly practised his faith there, and they could join in his worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/21-33.htm
